design_rationale: The study explicitly describes random allocation to exercise or control, stratified by NYHA class, with central randomization and concealed allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: Central, concealed randomization stratified by NYHA class was reported and observed group characteristics were broadly balanced, but the method used to generate the random sequence was not described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: To ensure balanced allocation of patients with heart disease across the two treatments groups, randomization was stratified by NYHA class. Allocation concealment was ensured by central randomization and nominal communication of patient allocation in the two arms of the study across the whole recruitment phase of the trial.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and personnel were necessarily unblinded, adherence varied substantially, and exercise-arm patients received ongoing encouragement and feedback, although intention-to-treat analyses with imputation were reported for the primary outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The trial was designed as a randomized, unblinded trial... dialysis nurses throughout the whole trial encouraged patients randomized to the exercise arm to keep an adequate adherence to the exercise prescription, and provided daily feedback to patients... We used intention-to-treat analyses for both the primary study outcomes (the 6MWT and the 5STS).

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 227 of 296 randomized participants (77%) were retested at six months, with greater attrition in the exercise arm, but the primary analyses used intention-to-treat methods and imputed missing longitudinal outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: 227 of 296 patients (77%) could be retested after 6 months (104 in the active arm... and 123 in the control arm...)... Missing longitudinal 6MWT and 5STS data were imputed along with recommendations made for the analysis of longitudinal data.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary physical-performance measures were appropriate and standardized across groups, but assessors were not kept blinded and performance could plausibly be influenced by awareness of allocation; questionnaire assistance was blinded when needed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Assessment was always performed on a nondialysis day by members of the rehabilitation team... No encouragement was allowed during the testing sessions... no special measure was adopted to keep them blind to patient allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: A trial registration and prespecified outcome categories are reported, but the supplied report does not establish that a prespecified statistical analysis plan was finalized before unblinded analysis, and numerous quality-of-life domains and both ITT and completer analyses create scope for selective emphasis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The protocol of the EXCITE trial (Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT01255969)... The primary outcome of the EXCITE study was functional capacity changes... assessed by the 6MWT and the 5STS... and changes in quality of life as measured by the KDQOL-SF.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged as some concerns. The main issues are incomplete reporting of sequence generation, substantial and differential attrition despite imputation, an unblinded behavioral intervention with variable adherence, unblinded physical-performance assessment, and residual uncertainty about selective reporting.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly assigned to test and control groups using a computerized random number generator.

domain_judgments.rationale: The sequence was generated randomly, but allocation concealment was not described; reported baseline characteristics were broadly similar, although some imbalances were present.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Patients fulfilling the inclusion criteria were divided randomly into a test group and a control group using a computerized random number generator.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and staff necessarily knew whether cycling or stretching was performed, and the analysis excluded four randomized participants rather than clearly using intention-to-treat, although attrition was balanced and no intervention-related deviations were reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Four patients were withdrawn from the study: in the test group one patient underwent a kidney transplant and one patient was transferred to another hospital for haemodialysis treatment; in the control group one patient was unwilling to continue and one patient died from an unrelated cause (Figure 1). Therefore, 65 patients completed the whole study

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 65 of 69 randomized participants (94.2%), with nearly identical dropout proportions between groups and reasons unlikely to depend jointly on true outcomes and assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Therefore, 65 patients completed the whole study, giving a completion rate of 94.2% and drop-out rates in the test and control groups of 5.9% and 5.7%, respectively.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessment was not reported as blinded, and both performance tests and self-reported HRQoL could be influenced by participants' and research staff's knowledge of treatment assignment, especially because staff guided questionnaire completion.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The questionnaire was completed by the patients themselves under the guidance of the research staff at the start of the study and after 12 weeks.

domain_judgments.rationale: No protocol or prespecified analysis plan was reported, numerous exercise-capacity and KDQOL-SF outcomes were tested, and the analysis used multiple within- and between-group comparisons without a stated multiplicity strategy, creating substantial scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Comparisons between and within the groups were made using independent-samples Student’s t-test for continuous variables and χ2-test for numerical data. A P-value <0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by unblinded assessment of subjective and effort-dependent outcomes and substantial potential for selective reporting across many outcomes and analyses without a protocol. Additional concerns arise from unreported allocation concealment and a complete-case rather than clearly intention-to-treat analysis.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports random assignment of 79 participants to four factorial groups by a research pharmacist using variable block sizes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation used variable-block randomization administered by an independent research pharmacist, concealment was maintained until assignment, and reported baseline characteristics did not show important imbalances.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups in a 1:1:1:1 manner by the research pharmacist using variable block sizes, which were not known to investigators until the completion of the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Drug allocation was blinded and adherence was high, but exercise assignment necessarily was unblinded, six participants stopped study injections, and the available-case analysis was not a full intention-to-treat analysis, although four treatment discontinuers remained in follow-up.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: For the analysis of outcomes, all available data were analyzed according to the original treatment assignment.

domain_judgments.rationale: Eleven of 79 randomized participants did not complete the study and only available outcome data were analyzed, while no sensitivity analysis or evidence demonstrating that missingness could not bias results was reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Sixty-eight patients completed the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary outcomes were measured with appropriate objective methods applied consistently, but assessor blinding—especially for exercise assignment—is not reported, and training-specific 3RM strength testing could be influenced by knowledge of assignment or familiarity with the exercise.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Primary outcomes included change in lean body mass (LBM) measured by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, quadriceps muscle cross-sectional area measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and knee extensor muscle strength.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, and numerous primary and secondary outcomes and possible analyses were available, creating scope for selective reporting despite generally comprehensive tables.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Primary outcomes included change in lean body mass (LBM) measured by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, quadriceps muscle cross-sectional area measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and knee extensor muscle strength. Secondary outcomes included changes in physical performance, self-reported physical functioning, and physical activity.

overall_summary: The randomization and allocation-concealment procedures were strong, but the trial raises some concerns because exercise assignment was unblinded, outcomes were analyzed using available data after 11 of 79 participants did not complete the study, assessor blinding was not reported, and no preregistration or analysis plan was provided. No domain was judged high risk.

design_rationale: The provided Methods/Participants text does not explicitly describe random allocation to the progressive-resistance and low-intensity aerobic exercise conditions; under the prespecified rule, unclear assignment must be classified as non-randomized.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation was not reported as random, and the available text gives no evidence that prognostic differences between the exercise groups (such as age, comorbidity, baseline function, dialysis clinic, or motivation) were controlled, creating substantial potential for confounding.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: This multicentric study included patients from Hospital General Universitario in Valencia (Spain) undertaking HD in two different HD clinics, Hospital General Universitario (11 patients) and Clínica Virgen del Consuelo (16 patients)

domain_judgments.domain_name: Bias due to selection of participants into the study
domain_judgments.rationale: Enrollment depended on medical-history review, nephrologist authorization, and subsequent solicitation of interest, while condition assignment is not described, so selection may have been related to health status and willingness to exercise, both of which plausibly affect outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All patients attending HD were evaluated for eligibility via medical history review and authorization from the patient’s nephrologist before solicitation of interest

domain_judgments.rationale: The two intended intervention categories were clearly identified as progressive resistance training and low-intensity aerobic exercise, making differential misclassification unlikely despite incomplete intervention details in the supplied excerpt.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: To compare the relative effects of PRT versus low-intensity aerobic exercise training on exercise capacity, strength, physical functioning and HRQoL.

domain_judgments.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_judgments.rationale: The interventions were necessarily unblinded exercise programs, and although an adherence section is listed, the supplied text does not report adherence, contamination, co-interventions, deviations, or whether analyses retained participants according to initial assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: 3.5. ADHERENCE TO EXERCISE PROGRAM .... 66

domain_judgments.rationale: A participant flowchart is listed, but the supplied text does not provide attrition numbers, reasons for missingness, or methods for handling missing outcome data, so bias from incomplete follow-up cannot be excluded.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Figure 1. Participants Flowchart ....71

domain_judgments.rationale: The study used established objective performance tests and the SF-36 across groups, but assessor blinding is not reported and self-reported quality of life could be influenced by participants' knowledge of their exercise condition.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote:
3.3.a. Sit to Stand to Sit Test (STS 10 and STS 60).... 60
3.3.b. 6 Minutes Walking Test (6MWT).... 60
3.3.e. Medical Outcomes Survey short form (SF-36).... 62

domain_judgments.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified analysis plan is reported, while numerous outcome measures, SF-36 subscales, time comparisons, and potential analyses were available, providing substantial scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Improve HRQoL, as measured by the SF-36 (8 scales and 2 components).

overall_summary: Overall ROBINS-I risk is serious, driven by non-randomized/unclear assignment with inadequate information about control of confounding, potentially selective enrollment, and substantial analytical and outcome-reporting flexibility without a reported protocol. Missing-data, deviations, and outcome-measurement safeguards were also insufficiently reported.

design_rationale: This was a parallel-group randomized controlled trial, and the Methods explicitly state that eligible patients were assigned using a computer-generated randomization list.

domain_judgments.rationale: The sequence was explicitly computer-generated and measured baseline characteristics appeared similar, but allocation concealment until enrollment and assignment was not described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Eligible patients were randomized into two groups using a computer-generated randomization list.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention personnel could not be blinded to exercise, and although sessions were supervised, adherence, crossover, co-interventions, and intention-to-treat handling were not clearly reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Intervention group patients received 4 training sessions per week for a period of 4 months.

domain_judgments.rationale: The same 41 randomized participants (20 control and 21 intervention) were represented in baseline and final outcome analyses, with complete ANOVA degrees of freedom and no reported attrition, indicating outcomes were available for nearly all participants.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Intervention group consisted of 21 exercising male patients and control group consisted of 20 non-exercising male patients.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessment was standardized and the investigator was blinded, but several patient-reported outcomes such as SF-36 and HADS could have been influenced by participants' unavoidable knowledge of exercise assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All assessments were performed by the same experienced investigator who was blinded as to the patients group assignment.

domain_judgments.rationale: No prospective registration or prespecified statistical analysis plan was reported, while numerous outcomes and both conventional and magnitude-based analyses created scope for selective reporting, although the reported outcomes generally matched those described in Methods.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Data were analyzed using a mixed measures (group × period) analysis of variance (ANOVA) for repeated measures.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is some concerns. The computer-generated randomization and blinded outcome assessor support validity, but allocation concealment, intervention adherence/analysis approach, susceptibility of self-reported outcomes to participant awareness, and protection against selective reporting were insufficiently documented.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly assigned to exercise or control using a random mechanism: a coin flip.

domain_judgments.rationale: A coin flip generated a random allocation, but concealment of the sequence/flip until assignment was not described, and the authors noted some baseline variability between groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After completion of all assessments at baseline, patients were randomly assigned to either an exercise training group (ET; 26 patients) or control group (C; 22 patients) by flip of a coin.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and personnel necessarily knew allocation, and the efficacy analysis excluded 15 of 48 randomized participants rather than using intention-to-treat, including withdrawal for loss of interest and non-compliance that could be intervention-related.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Of the 48 patients initially recruited, 33 patients finished the 3-month training and control observation period and had all the assessments repeated (31% drop out).

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were unavailable for 31% of randomized participants, with several potentially outcome-related reasons such as loss of interest, non-compliance, frailty, illness, and death, and no analysis showed that missingness could not bias results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Of the 48 patients initially recruited, 33 patients finished the 3-month training and control observation period and had all the assessments repeated (31% drop out).

domain_judgments.rationale: The physiological and functional outcome methods were objective, standardized, and applied similarly across groups, but assessor blinding was not reported and effort-dependent exercise and functional testing could be influenced by knowledge of allocation.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Each subject performed an incremental exercise test on a friction braked cycle ergometer (Monark 814, Monark exercise AB, Varberg, Sweden) for the determination of VO2 peak and VT.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan was reported, and numerous outcome measures and operationalizations were analyzed, leaving scope for selective reporting despite presentation of many results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Functional capacity was assessed using a variety of objective measures.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because 31% of randomized participants were excluded from the reported complete-case analyses, with potentially intervention- and outcome-related reasons for missingness and no intention-to-treat analysis. Additional concerns arise from unreported allocation concealment and assessor blinding, and lack of a prespecified analysis plan.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports 1:1 random assignment using customized randomization software, with randomization conducted separately by hospital.

domain_judgments.rationale: A software-generated, hospital-stratified random sequence was used and outcome baselines were broadly similar, but allocation concealment was not described and a significant baseline imbalance occurred for one functional-capacity measure.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The randomization procedure was completed using customized randomization software. ... Patients were randomized separately based on the host hospital.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily experienced resistance or its absence and adherence was not systematically recorded, although both groups received supervised cycling and all randomized patients reportedly completed follow-up; intention-to-treat analysis was not explicitly stated.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A limited number of exercise sessions were characterized as ‘incomplete’ ... Unfortunately, those events were not systematically recorded, thus we are unable to comment on whether the level of compliance ... could affect the final outcomes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data appear available for all 24 randomized participants because all patients completed the six-month program and group results retain n=12 per arm.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All of the patients successfully completed the 6-month intervention programme with no adverse effects and no augmentation phenomena to report.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary RLS outcome used a validated scale and assessments were timed consistently, but it was subjective and the report does not clearly state that outcome assessors were blinded; participants could distinguish resistance from no resistance.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The severity of the symptoms was assessed using the IRLSSG severity rating scale.

domain_judgments.rationale: A trial registration number is provided, but the report does not establish prospective registration or a prespecified analysis plan, and multiple outcomes and analysis approaches were available.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Clinical Trial Registry number. NCT00942253.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged as some concerns. Although randomization used software and complete outcome data were reported, allocation concealment, assessor blinding, systematic adherence recording, and prospective prespecification of reported analyses were insufficiently documented.

design_rationale: The Methods explicitly state that participants were randomly assigned by drawing lots to aquatic exercise or control, which is an explicit random allocation mechanism.

domain_judgments.rationale: Drawing lots is a valid random sequence method and the limited reported baseline characteristics were similar, but the paper does not describe who generated the lots or whether allocation was concealed until enrollment and assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: They were randomly assigned by simple allocation (drawing lots) to either a 4-month therapeutic aquatic exercise program (Group A-15 patients), or control status (Group B- 12 patients).

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they attended supervised aquatic training, adherence of at least 80% was required, and the analysis appears restricted to completers rather than intention-to-treat, although no specific intervention-related deviations were reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Patients were required to atend at least 80% of all sessions over the four-month period.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 27 of 29 randomized participants (93.1%), but two participants were excluded from the reported complete-case analysis and their assigned groups were not stated, leaving some uncertainty about attrition bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Two patients dropped out of the study due to lack of interest and for personal reasons (family health issues).

domain_judgments.rationale: Several performance outcomes required participant effort and assessor timing or instruction, and quality of life was self-reported; because participants knew their assignment and assessor blinding was not reported, outcome measurement could plausibly have been influenced differentially by intervention knowledge.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were instructed to perform the task “as fast as possible”

domain_judgments.rationale: No prospective protocol or preregistered analysis plan is reported, and numerous functional tests and SF-36 scales permit multiple eligible outcome measurements and analyses, although tables report the principal stated outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Six Minute Walk tests, Sit to Stand test, Sit and Reach test, Handgrip test, Timed Up and Go test were evaluated. All participants also completed SF-36 Questionnaire.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by unblinded measurement of effort-dependent functional outcomes and self-reported quality of life, with no assessor blinding reported. Additional concerns arise from unclear allocation concealment, complete-case rather than clearly intention-to-treat analysis, and absence of a prespecified protocol or analysis plan.
